passage:
After dinner at home, Anand looked up from the sofa. "Karthik, why are you checking your phone every five minutes?"
"It's the match, Anand bhaiya. I've got a bit riding on it."
"A bit?"
"Just a small bet. On the app."
"You said that last month. And the month before."
Karthik looked away. "I'm about to win back what I lost."
"How much did you lose?"
Silence. Then, "More than my stipend."
"Karthik."
"I know. I know. Every time I lose, I think the next one will fix it. And when I win, I want to bet more."
"That sounds like a trap."
"It is." His voice cracked. "I don't know how to stop."
Anand sat down beside his younger brother. "Okay. We'll find help. The counselling centre does this. I'll come."
Karthik nodded, and deleted the app while Anand watched.

qa.q: How much had Karthik lost?
qa.a: He had lost more than his stipend.

qa.q: What does Karthik's cracking voice reveal about his feelings?
qa.a: It reveals he feels trapped and ashamed, knowing the betting is out of control but not knowing how to stop.

qa.q: What made Anand's response helpful?
qa.a: He named the pattern calmly, didn't shame Karthik, and offered to go with him to get professional help.

qa.q: How might Anand feel, as Karthik's older brother, hearing about the losses?
qa.a: Anand is likely worried and shaken, but he stays calm and offers to come along, so Karthik feels able to accept help instead of hiding.

grounding: It shows a young man recognising a gambling dependence loop and taking a first step to exit it with his older brother's help.

passage: I didn't think gaming could be a problem until it was. I'm Shreya. In second year, I started playing online after classes. Then through dinner. Then through the night. I told myself I could stop anytime. I skipped my brother Siddharth's birthday call because I was mid-match. That's when I felt sick about it. I tried to quit on my own, but I'd last two days, feel restless, and go back. It was like my brain needed it. Finally I told a college counsellor. She helped me see the loop: stress, play, relief, guilt, more stress. We made a plan with blocked hours and things to do instead, like evening walks with a friend. I still play sometimes. But I choose when.

qa.q: Whose birthday call did Shreya skip?
qa.a: She skipped her brother Siddharth's birthday call.

qa.q: Why did Shreya feel sick after skipping the call?
qa.a: She realised gaming was pushing out the people she loved, which made her see the habit was out of control.

qa.q: How did the counsellor help Shreya exit the loop?
qa.a: She helped her understand the cycle of stress, play, relief and guilt, and plan blocked hours and alternative activities.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel about Shreya's change?
qa.a: Siddharth may have been hurt by the missed call; now that Shreya chooses when she plays, there may be more room for calls with him.

grounding: A young woman reflects on a gaming dependence loop and how she exited it with professional help.

passage:
College counsellor's note:
Jatin, 21, came in after his friend Gopika urged him to. He said he drinks "a bit" most nights to fall asleep and to cope with stress about exams. Over the last few months he's needed more to feel the same, and he feels anxious and shaky when he skips it. He missed two exams. He was defensive at first, saying "everyone drinks in college." When I asked what he wanted his life to look like in a year, he became quiet and said, "Not like this."
We discussed the cycle of stress, drinking, worse sleep and more stress. I referred him to the campus doctor and a support group. Next steps: weekly sessions. He asked if Gopika could come to the first support meeting.

qa.q: How many exams did Jatin miss?
qa.a: He missed two exams.

qa.q: What does Jatin's "Not like this" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests that under his defensiveness, he was unhappy with where his drinking was taking him and wanted to change.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do that was helpful?
qa.a: The counsellor didn't argue with his defensiveness but asked about his future, explained the cycle, and referred him to a doctor and support group.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel when Jatin asks Gopika to come to the support meeting?
qa.a: Gopika might feel relieved and trusted, glad the urging led Jatin to get help.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a young man recognising an alcohol dependence loop and starting professional help.

passage:
Friday night
Lost again. Not a huge amount, but it was my mess money for the month, and I only meant to play 'one round' of that online card game after dinner. I keep doing the same thing: lose, feel sick, play again to win it back, win a little, feel great, play more. It's a loop and I'm the hamster in the wheel. Tarun saw me on my phone at 2 am last week and asked if I was okay. I lied and said I was chatting. Today I told him the truth. He didn't lecture. He just said, 'Let's deal with it, Nilesh.' So: uninstalled the app, gave Tarun my debit card to keep for now, and tomorrow I'm calling Maa, even though I'm dreading it. Tarun also found a helpline for gambling problems. I saved the number. Scared. Also lighter.

qa.q: What money did Nilesh lose?
qa.a: The mess money for the month.

qa.q: How does Nilesh feel at the end of the entry, and what shows it?
qa.a: Scared and lighter at once; Nilesh dreads calling Maa, yet telling Tarun and taking steps has eased the weight of the secret.

qa.q: Which steps help Nilesh break the loop?
qa.a: Removing the app, putting the debit card out of easy reach, planning to tell family and saving a helpline number give barriers and support instead of willpower alone.

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt when Nilesh told him the truth?
qa.a: Perhaps a little hurt about the earlier lie, but mostly concerned and glad to be trusted, which is why he said, 'Let's deal with it.' 🤍

grounding: A diary entry shows a student recognising a gambling dependence loop and taking first steps to exit it with support.

passage:
Himani: can I tell you something without you freaking out
Pallavi: always
Himani: I think I'm drinking too much. it started with weekend parties. now it's most nights, alone, to switch my brain off
Himani: I skipped the lab test today bc I felt awful
Pallavi: thank you for telling me. not freaking out
Pallavi: does it feel hard to stop on the nights you try?
Himani: yeah. I tell myself not tonight and then 11 pm happens
Pallavi: ok. want to do evenings together this week? I'll come over after class, we cook, walk, whatever
Himani: yes please
Pallavi: and the college counsellor sees students privately. I can come with you to book
Himani: scared they'll judge me
Pallavi: they hear this a lot. you'd be getting help early, not failing
Himani: ok. tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Himani skip because of feeling awful?
qa.a: The lab test.

qa.q: Why did Himani begin with 'without you freaking out'?
qa.a: Himani was afraid of being judged or causing alarm, which shows how much shame Himani felt about the drinking.

qa.q: What makes Pallavi's replies helpful?
qa.a: Pallavi stays calm, asks how it feels instead of lecturing, offers company in the hard evenings and points to the counsellor while offering to go along.

qa.q: How might Pallavi be feeling during the chat?
qa.a: Likely worried underneath but careful to keep a steady tone, so that Himani keeps talking and takes the next step.

grounding: A chat shows a student recognising an alcohol dependence loop and a friend helping Himani toward support and a way out.
